title: Sequences From Step Changes
statement:
A sequence of n + 1 whole numbers was lost. All you kept is steps, where steps[i] is how much the sequence changed from position i to position i + 1, and the fact that every number in it was between low and high, inclusive.

Return how many different sequences fit that description. It may be 0.

examples.why: Starting at s, the values are s, s+2, s−1, s. They must all lie in [0, 4], so s ≥ 1 and s ≤ 2. The dip to s−1 matters even though the sequence ends where it started.
The values climb 5 above the start at one point, but the allowed range is only 3 wide.
A flat sequence fits for every start from −3 to 3.

hints: Once you pick the first number, the whole sequence is fixed. So you are counting valid starting values.
Write every value as start + (running sum of steps so far). The constraint only cares about the smallest and the largest running sum.
If the running sums (including 0 for the start) span from mn to mx, the start needs low − mn ≤ start ≤ high − mx. Count the integers in that range, and never return a negative count.

explain.intuition:
The steps fix the shape of the sequence; only the starting value is free. Value i is start + prefix[i], where prefix is the running sum of steps with prefix[0] = 0. Sliding the start up or down moves the whole shape rigidly.

The shape fits in [low, high] exactly when its lowest point and highest point do. With mn and mx the smallest and largest running sums, the start must satisfy start + mn ≥ low and start + mx ≤ high. That is an interval of starts with (high − low) − (mx − mn) + 1 integers, or none if the shape is taller than the range.
steps: Set sum = mn = mx = 0 (the start itself is a point of the shape).
For each step, add it to sum and update mn and mx.
pitfalls: Forgetting the starting point. With steps = [3] the running sums are 0 and 3, a span of 3, not 0.
Only checking where the sequence ends. In the first example the end equals the start, but the dip in the middle still cuts the count.
In fixed-width languages, a running sum of 100 000 steps of 100 000 overflows 32-bit integers. Use 64-bit.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: For each start from low to high, walk the steps and check every value stays in range.

solutions.title: Span of the running sum
solutions.idea: The steps fix the sequence's shape; the count is how many vertical positions of that shape fit in the range.

followups: Some steps are unknown, only bounded between −k and k. How would you check whether any sequence fits?
Answer many (low, high) queries for the same steps. What do you precompute?
